doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Head arrangements, lost royalties and the $41.25 session fee
summary: Early sessions used made-up heads whose players never got royalties; Marty remembers the scale pay.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well it’s interesting that a lot of recording at that time must have been pretty much off the cuff. You get the musicians together and then you decide what you’re going to play.

Oh that’s what it was. So everything was mostly head arrangements, that’s how they started those heads. But the thing was, what was bad about it was the promoters, who knew nothing about music, but they just happened to know the musicians, they would get them in the studio and they would say “just make something up.” And they would make something up and then somebody would come up with a name for the song, and the guys
would never get any royalties for it. So now there’s a couple of guys, friends of mine now, they’re let me see, Dean Pratt and Don Sickler. Do you know those names?

Don Sickler is a publisher and he’s got this music composer’s something, and they look out for royalties for musicians who’ve been getting screwed over the years, not getting their just desserts. And they’re beautiful, because they look out for musicians and make sure they get what they’re supposed to get you see? So that’s what happened. A lot of those little things where the guys made up a little head arrangement and nobody ever saw any money for it, except the guy who was running the record company.
What would a record date like that pay?
In those days, for a three hour session, forty-one and a quarter. $41.25.
You do have a pretty good memory.
